resources.string: See what a photo is carrying
Photos usually record where and when they were taken and which device took them. Pick one to see what is in it, then export a copy without any of it.
This photo records where it was taken.
This photo records details that identify your device.
This photo carries some metadata, none of it locating.
No metadata found in this photo.
Where the photo was taken, usually accurate to a few metres.
Which camera took it. Some cameras include a serial number, which ties every photo you have ever shared to the same body.
When it was taken, usually to the second and often with your timezone.
Names, copyright and the app that edited it.
Exposure and lens details. Describes the shot rather than you.

A small copy of the image is stored inside the file. It is made when the photo is taken and is not always updated when the photo is edited — so a cropped or blurred photo can still carry a preview of the original.
The clean copy is not saved to your gallery. It is held only for sharing, and replaced the next time you export.
Checked: the exported file is clean
Also removed an embedded video of about %1$d kB. Some phones record a few seconds of motion with every photo.
Also removed %1$d kB of data stored after the end of the image.
The image itself is untouched — not re-saved, not recompressed.
This copy was re-saved, so the image quality is slightly lower than the original.
The file name contains a date, so the copy will be renamed.
%1$s files cannot be cleaned without re-saving the image. Converting produces a JPEG with no metadata, at slightly lower quality than the original.
No map app on this device.
This photo had no metadata to remove.
That photo could not be opened.
That file is too large for this tool to work on.
That file is not an image this tool can read.
Something survived the clean-up, so the copy was not offered. This file has an unusual structure — please do not treat it as stripped.
The clean copy could not be written. There may not be enough free space.

A colour profile describes how colours in the file should be interpreted. It says nothing about you, your camera or where you were. Removing it makes the file marginally smaller and can make photos look washed out or oversaturated in some apps, so it is kept by default.

Everything except the parts needed to display the image. That means location, dates, camera make and model, serial numbers, editing history, captions, comments, the embedded preview, and any block this tool does not recognise — including manufacturer-specific data, which is where cameras tend to hide serial numbers. Anything stored after the end of the image is removed too; some phones append a short video to every photo.

Orientation, and the colour profile if you leave it switched on. Orientation is a single number from 1 to 8 that tells an app which way up to show the photo. Without it, pictures taken in portrait come out sideways. It reveals nothing about you.\n\nThe image itself is copied across byte for byte. Nothing is re-saved or recompressed, so the clean copy is exactly as sharp as the original — the file is simply smaller.

This removes information stored alongside the image. It cannot remove anything hidden inside the picture itself — a visible or invisible watermark, or a pattern deliberately encoded into the pixels — because that is part of the image, and removing it would mean changing what the photo looks like.

It also cannot control what happens after you share. Some services add their own metadata, and some keep a copy of what you upload.

HEIC files, which many phones now use by default, can be inspected but not cleaned without re-saving them.
